Debtors

Everyone who owes you, oldest money first

Every customer carrying a balance, with the age of the money beside it. A balance is the charges not yet paid, walked oldest first the way a ledger settles — so the age here is the age of the money still open, not the date the customer last came in. The bands split the whole book by age and narrow the list when you tap one; the search box narrows it further; the printed sheet always carries the whole book's profile and says which customers it is listing. Receiving a payment clears their oldest invoice first and posts straight to the cash book. Asking for the money is a different screen: Chase debts has everyone past your terms with the words already written, and nothing sends itself.

Consignment

Goods on your shelf that are not yours, and what has sold of them

Goods a supplier has left with you to sell and be paid for as they sell. They sit on your shelf and can be sold like anything else — but they are not yours, so they are not counted in what your stock is worth, and the moment one sells, part of the money in the drawer belongs to whoever left it. That running figure is what this screen exists for. Settling raises an ordinary supplier bill for what has sold, which you then pay the usual way; unsold goods can go back at any time, owing nothing.

Pricing

What your shelf keeps, and what it is not selling

Every line that is losing you money, worst first. Two kinds sit on one list: a line you are selling too cheaply, where the fix is to charge more, and a line that is not selling at all, where the fix is to take less and offer it to somebody who has bought it before. Their figures are different money — a thin line’s repeats every month, dead stock’s comes back once — so nothing here ever adds them together, each row says which it is, and the order is worked out on one clock: what a fix would be worth over a year. Opening a line shows the arithmetic behind it, so you can check the figure rather than take it. Nothing changes until you tap it and confirm it, and no offer is ever sent by the app.

Chase debts

Past the shop's terms, worst-aged first, each message written from their own invoices. Nothing sends itself.

Everyone whose balance is past the shop's terms, worst-aged first, each with a message already written from their own invoices. Nobody is chased inside the grace period, nobody is chased twice in the same few days, and a customer whose balance does not agree with its own history is held back for checking rather than asked for a figure the shop cannot explain. Read the message, change it if you like, then send it with your own thumb — the app never sends anything by itself.

Chase after 7 days · rest 3 days
When a debt becomes a chase Nobody is asked inside the grace period, and nobody is asked twice inside the rest period — so a customer is never chased two days running.

Creditors

What you owe, and how far today's cash reaches

Every supplier carrying a balance, ordered by who to pay first: a day you named and let pass, then days you have given, then whoever has been kept waiting longest. The strip leads with what is in hand today, because what you owe is only half a sentence — the question is always what can be paid now. A dashed line across the list marks how far today's cash reaches if you pay down the list in full; when the cash book has not been opened there is no line, because there is no figure to measure against. The bands split the whole book by age and narrow the list when you tap one. Opening a supplier shows the bills behind the figure, and each bill is where you name the day you will pay it — that day puts the bill on the cash line in What's coming and drops what you can safely spend, and a bill with no day stays off that line rather than have a date invented for it. Paying settles that supplier's oldest bill first and posts straight to the cash book.

Staff

Who you can hand the next order to.

The people who pick and deliver for you, ordered by who is free: anybody idle first, then whoever is carrying least, then people who cannot be sent work at all. A row carries only what decides whether this person gets the next order — whether they are free, what they can do, and the one figure that speaks to their work — and opens in place for the rest of their record. Every figure is counted from the orders themselves over the period named on the control above the list; nothing is stored and nothing is ranked. Nothing here hands anybody an order: that happens on Order tracking, and it is always a tap of yours. The month of days at the foot is the same register the payroll screen docks from — there is no second attendance record and no second figure to reconcile. Which devices are signed in moved to Presets, under Signed-in devices; what matters about it here is on the person’s own row, as “No app login”.

Price registry

What suppliers quote, what you actually paid, and what other shops charge.

Every quote you've collected, one card per supplier's price for a line. Read it while you quote; tick a price you have checked and found unchanged. Add an entry each time a supplier gives you a price — wholesale and retail. Under the two prices each card carries what you last paid that supplier, read from your own purchase invoices, and what the nearest rival charges, read from the sightings on file — as marks rather than words. The key under the counts says what each mark means. Paid switches to what each supplier has actually charged you, read from your own purchase invoices and ranked by money rather than percentage, with the rows where the registry no longer matches what you pay first. Prices are only ever compared against prices for the same unit, and a single purchase is never called a trend. Rivals switches to what other shops sell your lines for — every figure something a person saw, with the day — and where being dearer is costing you most.

What's coming

What you have already promised, against what you hold

The line starts at what the cash book says you hold this morning and steps down on each day something you have already promised falls due. It is a step rather than a slope because money does not drain away between payments — it sits still and then goes. Safe to spend is the LOWEST point the line reaches, not what it ends on: ending the month with something left is no comfort if you are under water in the middle of it, and the buying plan budgets from that lowest figure. Only money with a day somebody actually named is on the line; everything else is counted below it, undated, and each becomes part of the line the day you name one. A debtor's word is drawn too, dashed, and is never counted in what is safe to spend.

Payroll & rent

What goes out to your people and your landlord, and how far today's cash reaches

Every wage and every rent for the month on screen, in the order the money has to leave: anything already late first, then whatever falls due soonest — wages all land on the last day of the month, so they arrive together — then the largest month within one day, because that is the one today’s cash decides. The strip leads with what is in hand, because what you owe is only half a sentence on payday; the question is whether it can be paid. A dashed line across the list marks how far today’s cash reaches if you pay down the list in order, and when the cash book has not been opened there is no line rather than one drawn from a figure nobody recorded. Opening a month shows how it was worked out — the days, the rate, every day missed and what it cost — and it is where the days are entered and where the month is paid. Paying asks which account the money leaves and posts it straight to the Cash Book under Rent or Salaries & Wages. Nothing here pays anybody on its own, and no month is raised by being looked at.

Default price rule

The selling rule for every product that has none of its own. A product without a markup rule cannot be sold by the counter, the assistant, or the catalogues — this fills that gap in one move. A rule set on a product (or a variant) always wins over this default, and clearing it drops the product back here.

When no rule is set on the product

Percent adds on top of the item's cheapest supplier cost and scales with the item — the safe choice across a whole catalogue. Fixed adds a flat amount: per pack on the wholesale side, per piece on retail, the same way product rules work. A product with no supplier cost on file still cannot be priced by any rule — there is nothing to add on top of. Leave a side at 0 for no default on that side.

Agent terms

What share of your margin external sales agents get, and how long a product must sit in their cluster before it earns a bonus.

Default share of margin

A percentage of what you make on an item, not off its price — 50% gives an agent half your margin, 100% gives all of it and they pay exactly your cost. Below cost is not reachable, whatever is set here. Any product can override either one in its own edit form; this is the fallback when it does not.

Cluster bonus

How long a product must already have been in an agent's commission cluster before a sale of it earns the bonus. Stops an agent starring a high-bonus item right before checkout just to collect on it.

Order timing

If an order sits in one of these steps on the Order Tracking board longer than its limit, its card gets a blinking warning flag. Leave a step blank or 0 to turn its warning off.

Only while the app is open. This shop's notifications reach a picker's phone through their worker app; there is no such channel for you, so a closed browser cannot be reached. Keep the app open on the counter machine and it works all day. Set at least one limit above, or there is nothing to go past.

Price checking

The registry refreshes itself only where the shop is busy — quoting an item, restocking it, receiving it — so anything you do not trade regularly is never questioned again. These two settings drive the Prices To Check report on the dashboard. Where an item has enough dated purchase invoices to show how fast its own price moves, that is used instead of the limit below; where it has not, the limit below applies.

Signed-in devices

Every phone and computer signed in to this shop, and when it was last heard from. Signing a device out takes effect the next time it checks in.

Shop identity

What prints at the top of a receipt. Until now every printout carried the shop's name and nothing else — a receipt handed across the counter has to say where it came from and how to come back. Leave a field blank and its line simply does not print.

To print with no dialog, make a desktop shortcut to Chrome with --kiosk-printing after the program path, and open the app from it. Receipts then go straight to the default printer. Set the 80mm thermal printer as the Windows default first.
Paper: 80mm roll, 72mm printed. The receipt is only as long as its contents, so short sales use short paper.

What to buy

Ranked by what each line earned in 30 days. Nothing is ordered until you send it.

What is worth buying, worked out from the shop's own records and ranked by what each thing actually earned in the last 30 days. Two kinds of line: a shelf refill, for goods that sold off our own stock and are running low, and worth stocking, for goods bought in order after order and never held — where the price on file for the whole month's quantity in one buy is compared with what was really paid across those separate buys. Each line says why in plain words, and names the cheapest supplier at the quantity needed, volume discounts included. The budget starts at the cash on hand; what does not fit is named rather than dropped. Nothing here is a forecast — every figure comes from an invoice or the Price Registry.
